literal: " Commentary: This juan too was supplemented from the corresponding biographies in Beishi juan 15, Imperial Clan of Wei; occasionally there are superfluous words and sentences that must come from the Gaoshi xiaoshi.
idiomatic: Note: This scroll was likewise patched from the parallel lives in Beishi juan 15 (Wei imperial clan); stray phrases now and then surely come from Gaoshi xiaoshi.

literal: Died in the tenth year of Jianguo. Beishi juan 15, Imperial Clan of Wei, writes the "ten" of "ten years" as "fifteen years."
idiomatic: "Died Jianguo year 10": Beishi juan 15 (Wei imperial clan) reads "ten years" as "fifteen years."

literal: Commentary: Juan 13, Biographies of Empresses, says Empress Zhaocheng, née Murong, "gave birth to Emperor Xianming and the Prince of Qinming."
idiomatic: Note: Juan 13 (Empresses) says Murong, empress of Zhaocheng, bore Emperor Xianming and the Prince of Qinming.

literal: According to juan 1, Chronological Annals, in the sixth month, summer, of Jianguo year 7, Murong married Shiyijian, and moreover Han had an elder brother Shi; then in Jianguo year 10 whether Han had yet been born is still unknown—even death in year 15 would make him at most a child of six or seven, inconsistent with the biography's "at fifteen he requested to lead cavalry on campaign" and "when grown he commanded troops" and the like.
idiomatic: Juan 1's annals place Murong's marriage to Shiyijian in summer, sixth month, year 7 of Jianguo, and Han had an elder brother Shi; by year 10 his birth is uncertain, and even death in year 15 would leave him six or seven—far too young for "at fifteen he asked to lead horse on campaign" and "when grown he commanded armies."

literal: This biography says "died in Jianguo year 10," and Beishi says "died in year 15"—both are wrong.
idiomatic: Both this life ('died year 10') and Beishi ('died year 15') are in error.

literal: According to juan 13, Biography of Empress Xianming, née He, it says "the empress's younger son, Prince Gu of Qin"; according to this biography Gu was also Han's son—presumably after the Xianming Heir Apparent Tuoba Shi died, He adopted the children as born to Han's wife.
idiomatic: Juan 13 (Empress Xianming He) calls Gu the empress's younger son, Prince of Qin; this life makes Gu Han's son too—likely He adopted him after heir Tuoba Shi died, reckoning him Han's issue.

literal: Tuoba Shi died in Jianguo year 34, as seen in the Chronological Annals; Han's death must therefore have come after that.
idiomatic: Shi died in year 34 per the annals; Han cannot have died before that.

literal: Above and below the character "ten" there should be missing characters.
idiomatic: Characters are missing before and after "ten."

literal: His grandfather received the Jin calendar investiture. Commentary: By rites one may not call one's own grandfather "that grandfather"; the character "nai" is suspected to be a corruption of "ji" (and).
idiomatic: "His grandfather received Jin investiture": one may not style one's forebear "that grandfather" by ritual; nai likely corrupts ji (and).

literal: Granted a hand-drawn couch to treat him with especial favor. Cefu juan 277
idiomatic: "Granted a hand-drawn couch to honor him specially." Cefu juan 277
folio 3269

literal: On the page "ji" (couch) is written "che" (cart).
idiomatic: That folio reads che (cart) for ji (couch).

literal: It is suspected that after "ji" in this biography the character "zhang" (staff) is missing.
idiomatic: This life probably drops zhang (staff) after ji.

literal: Cefu, because it would not parse, changed "ji" to "che."
idiomatic: Cefu, finding the line unusable, emended ji to che.

literal: Held Hegu's pass in Bohai. Commentary: Juan 2, Annals of Taizu, first month of Tianxing year 1 says "Yuanyang Duke Yuan Zun garrisoned Hegu's pass in Bohai"; here "ling" (to hold/lead) should be the corruption "zhen" (to garrison).
idiomatic: "Held Hegu pass in Bohai": juan 2 (Taizu) has Yuan Zun "garrisoning" Hegu in the first month, Tianxing 1; ling should be zhen (garrison).

literal: Gaozu was about to mourn for Prince Jian of Qi commandery. In all editions and Beishi juan 15, Biography of Changshan Prince Zun, "Jian" is all written "Lan."
idiomatic: "Gaozu was to mourn Prince Jian of Qi": every edition and Beishi juan 15 (Changshan Prince Zun) write Jian as Lan.

literal: Commentary: This book juan 20 and Beishi juan 19 have biographies of Prince Jian of Qi commandery.
idiomatic: Note: This work juan 20 and Beishi juan 19 both carry lives of Prince Jian of Qi.

literal: That person died in Taihe year 23; Yuan Hong was already ill and for him "forced himself while ill to perform mourning."
idiomatic: He died in Taihe 23; Yuan Hong was already sick and "forced mourning despite illness."

literal: This book's Annals of Gaozu repeatedly mention him, all as "Jian."
idiomatic: Gaozu's annals in this book always read Jian.

literal: This biography was supplemented from Beishi, so it also inherits Beishi's error; now corrected according to the annals and the original biography.
idiomatic: Patched from Beishi, this life repeats Beishi's mistake; emended per the annals and the dedicated biography.

literal: "Entered the Directorate with weapons." Commentary: "entered the Directorate with weapons" cannot be parsed.
idiomatic: "Entered the Directorate with arms": the phrase will not parse.

literal: Beishi juan 6, Basic Annals of Qi, Upper, says "Sun Teng entered the Directorate with belt and weapons and on his own authority killed a censor."
idiomatic: Beishi juan 6 (Qi annals, upper) has Sun Teng "entering the Directorate armed and killing a censor on his own authority."

literal: One knows that above "zhan" (weapons) the character "dai" (bearing arms) should be missing.
idiomatic: Dai (bearing arms) must be missing before zhan.

literal: Sheng's younger brother Shouxing. Beishi juan 15 is the same; Tongzhi juan 84, this biography, makes it Sheng's younger brother Bing, courtesy name Shouxing."
idiomatic: "Sheng's younger brother Shouxing": Beishi juan 15 agrees; Tongzhi juan 84 has Sheng's younger brother Bing, styled Shouxing."

literal: Below, wherever this biography and Beishi read "Shouxing," Tongzhi all reads "Bing."
idiomatic: Every later "Shouxing" in this life and Beishi appears as "Bing" in Tongzhi.

literal: Below, on his deathbed Shouxing wrote his own epitaph saying: "A man of Luoyang, surname Yuan, personal name Jing.
idiomatic: Below, Shouxing's deathbed self-composed epitaph runs: "A Luoyang man, family Yuan, personal name Jing."

literal: " Tongzhi also writes "Jing" as "Bing."
idiomatic: " Tongzhi likewise gives Bing for Jing.

literal: Commentary: Muzhi jishi, Epitaph of Yuan Zhi
idiomatic: Note: Muzhi jishi, Epitaph of Yuan Zhi

literal: 〈plate 51〉
idiomatic: plate 51

literal: states "grandfather Bing, Bearer of the Staff, Regular Attendant of the Rapid Cavaliers, Commander of All Military Affairs in Xuzhou, General Who Pacifies the East, Inspector of Xuzhou, Director of the Imperial Clan."
idiomatic: names "Grandfather Bing, credential-bearing, Regular Cavalier Attendant, Commander of Xuzhou armies, General Pacifying the East, Xuzhou inspector, Director of the Imperial Clan."

literal: Earlier scholars by official title and genealogy proved that "Bing" is "Shouxing."
idiomatic: Earlier scholars identified Bing with Shouxing from titles and pedigree.

literal: Moreover juan 66, Biography of Cui Liang, also says the Xuzhou inspector he impeached was called "Yuan Bing."
idiomatic: Juan 66 (Cui Liang) likewise names the Xuzhou inspector he impeached Yuan Bing.

literal: Shouxing's personal name was "Bing."
idiomatic: Shouxing's true name was Bing.

literal: 〈same as Bing〉
idiomatic: same graph as Bing

literal: There is no doubt; Beishi uses the courtesy name to avoid Tang taboo, while in the self-composed epitaph, for rhyme's sake, "Bing" was changed to "Jing."
idiomatic: Beyond doubt: Beishi gives the style to dodge Tang taboo; the self-written epitaph rhymes Bing as Jing.

literal: Personal and place names of the time often used homophonous characters; some other books write Bing, and Zheng Qiao reverted the text accordingly.
idiomatic: Homophones were common in names; some texts read the name as Bing, and Zheng Qiao restored that reading.

literal: In the original Wei shu, according to the Cui Liang biography it ought to read "Bing."
idiomatic: Wei Shou's original, per Cui Liang, should read Bing.

literal: The hanging gate snapped and struck Ning at the waist
idiomatic: The gate mechanism broke and hit Ning's waist

idiomatic: text missing

literal: and emerged. Qian's Kaoyi juan 38 says: "Below 'yao' there is missing text; it should be yao
idiomatic: "and emerged." Qian Daxin, Kaoyi juan 38: "Text is missing after yao; yao likely continues as

idiomatic: belt or similar."

literal: Zhong's son Hui. Beishi juan 15 reads "Kui's younger brother Hui," making him the son of Zhong's younger brother De.
idiomatic: "Zhong's son Hui": Beishi juan 15 has "Kui's younger brother Hui," hence De's son, not Zhong's.

literal: Commentary: In the Shouxing biography above it says "cousin Hui."
idiomatic: Note: Shouxing's life above calls Hui a "cousin."

literal: Shouxing was Zhong's son; if Hui were also Zhong's son, how could he be called "cousin"?
idiomatic: Shouxing is Zhong's son; if Hui were too, "cousin" would be impossible.

literal: Moreover appended biographies by custom each follow their father or elder brother; Hui's biography is not placed after Zhong's biography but after De's biography—also proving he was De's son.
idiomatic: Supplement lives follow their paternal line; Hui's is filed after De's, not Zhong's—more proof he is De's son.

literal: Song Zhao Mingcheng, Jinshi lu juan 21, colophon to the stele of Yuan Hui, already said Wei shu and Beishi differ, "examining by the stele, Beishi is correct."
idiomatic: Zhao Mingcheng (Song), Jinshi lu juan 21, on Yuan Hui's stele already noted Wei shu disagrees with Beishi and concluded: "The stele proves Beishi right."

literal: Muzhi jishi, Epitaph of Yuan Hui
idiomatic: Yuan Hui's epitaph in Muzhi jishi

idiomatic: plate 55

idiomatic: calls his father "Jizhou inspector, Duke Jian of Hejian."

idiomatic: , shows "Duke Jian of Hejian" is the Yuan De of this life; Mou and the others name Yuan as De's son—Beishi correct, Wei shu not.
